## Resume essentials

Note: Northwind Analytics appears to be a fictional company created for this test fixture — a web search turned up no real organization by this name in logistics/route-planning software ([search results](https://www.esri.com/en-us/industries/logistics-distribution/strategies/route-planning-optimization), [Northwind Technology, an unrelated SAP oil-and-gas vendor](https://northwindtechnology.com/)). The advice below is based on the posting's own text and general, verifiable product-management practice, not on claims about this specific employer.

The posting repeatedly uses these words — mirror them on your resume: "customer interviews," "requirements," "user stories and acceptance criteria," "backlog prioritized," "product metrics (adoption, retention, time-to-plan)," "experiments," "coordinate releases."

- **Talking to customers / turning feedback into requirements.** Your PM Club events chair role and your moving-company internship (answering customer calls, logging complaints) both show direct customer contact. Call this out explicitly: "Logged and categorized customer complaints, surfacing recurring issues" — that is literally the "analyse support tickets to find problems worth solving" line from the posting.
- **Data and tracking.** You built a Google Sheets tracker for club sign-ups — use this to show the "comfort with data: spreadsheets required" requirement. Quantify it: attendance grew from 22 to 41 students across 5 events, which is a concrete, numeric result worth putting on the resume as-is.
- **Leading a project or team.** Events chair of the PM Club for two semesters is a direct match for "evidence of leading a project or team ... student club, internship or part-time job." State the scope (ran 5 events) and the outcome (attendance growth).
- **SQL.** The posting lists SQL as "a plus," not required — where your background does not show it, do not claim it. Instead, show you're closing the gap (see below) and lean on the spreadsheet evidence you do have.
- **Agile/Scrum, Jira.** Listed as "nice to have." Your background does not mention either. Note: rather than inventing experience, the honest move is to omit these from the resume and address them if raised in the interview (see "Handling your gaps").
- **Curiosity about logistics and supply chains.** Your moving-company internship is adjacent (operations, customer service in a logistics-adjacent business) — frame it that way rather than just "customer service job."

## Handling your gaps

**Gap 1: No SQL.**
Honest, confident framing: "I haven't used SQL in a work setting yet, but I'm comfortable with structured data — I built and maintained a Google Sheets tracker for my club that [your club] relied on for sign-ups — and I've started learning SQL because this role calls for it." This is honest (you have adjacent spreadsheet evidence, not SQL claims) and shows initiative rather than excuse-making.
Concrete step before the interview: Note: this is a step I'm suggesting, not something you've done — complete a short, free SQL fundamentals course (e.g., a basic SELECT/JOIN/WHERE module) and be ready to say specifically what you learned, so the claim "I've started learning SQL" is true when you say it.

**Gap 2: Never worked in software.**
Honest, confident framing: "My internships have been in operations and customer service, not software, but the core PM skill — turning what customers tell you into something a team can act on — is exactly what I did logging and categorizing complaints at [the moving company], and it's what I'd be doing here with support tickets." This reframes the gap as transferable skill rather than denying it.
Concrete step before the interview: Note: another suggested step, not something already done — read two or three posts on how APMs without engineering backgrounds succeed (for example on a product management blog or subreddit) and prepare one specific question for the interviewer about how the senior PM and engineers split requirements work, so you can speak to the team structure rather than just the title.

## Questions to prepare for

- "Walk me through a time you had to prioritize competing demands." — Tests whether you can talk through trade-offs methodically; your club event planning (budget, attendance, volunteer time) is fair game here.
- "How would you turn a pile of customer complaints into a prioritized backlog?" — Specific to this posting's "analyse support tickets" duty; shows whether you understand triage, not just listening.
- "Tell me about a metric you tracked and what you did when it didn't move the way you wanted." — Matches "track product metrics ... report on them monthly"; your attendance-growth tracker is a usable example if you can explain what you'd have done had attendance *not* grown.
- "Why product management, and why this industry (logistics)?" — Standard APM-round question; tests genuine interest versus a generic "I like building things" answer.
- "How do you explain a technical limitation to a non-technical customer?" — Directly lifted from "explain a technical trade-off to a non-technical customer"; shows communication skill, the posting's top listed requirement.
- "You don't have a software or SQL background — how do you expect to ramp up?" — Likely given your stated gaps; shows self-awareness and a concrete plan versus defensiveness.

## Smart questions to ask

- "The posting mentions shipping improvements every two weeks — what does the handoff between the PM, engineers, and designers look like day to day on this team?"
- "What does success look like for this role at the 6-month mark, versus the 12-month mark?"
- "You've grown 40% a year for three years — what's straining the most as the team scales, and does that show up in this role?" [unverified — growth figure is stated in the posting itself, not independently confirmed]
- "How does the team decide which customer-reported problems get turned into experiments versus straight into the backlog?"
- "What tools does the team use today for backlog and metrics tracking, and how set are those versus open to change?"
- "What's the balance between route-planning feature work and the coordination-with-sales-and-customer-success side of this role?"

## Summary

This resume and interview plan for the Northwind Analytics Associate Product Manager posting (fictional test company, applying for a role closing November 15, 2026) maps the candidate's PM Club leadership, attendance-tracking spreadsheet, and moving-company customer-service internship directly onto the posting's own language around customer interviews, backlog prioritization, and data tracking, while addressing two acknowledged gaps — no SQL and no software-industry experience — with honest framing plus a concrete pre-interview learning step for each.
